title: The Revolt of "Mother"
focus: a wife's quiet rebellion for a decent home

teacherSummary.text: For forty years Sarah Penn has waited for the new house her husband Adoniram promised. Instead he builds another barn. While he is away buying a horse, she moves the family and furniture into the new barn and makes it a home. Adoniram returns, is stunned, and weeps, saying he will put up partitions and windows: he never knew she was so set on it.

annotationFocus.passage: Sarah Penn's face as she rolled her pies had that expression of meek vigor which might have characterized one of the New Testament saints. She was making mince-pies. Her husband, Adoniram Penn, liked them better than any other kind. She baked twice a week. Adoniram often liked a piece of pie between meals. She hurried this morning. It had been later than usual when she began, and she wanted to have a pie baked for dinner. However deep a resentment she might be forced to hold against her husband, she would never fail in sedulous attention to his wants.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “What are they digging for, mother” slowly and put it in my own words: Sarah asks her husband what the workers are digging, and he will not answer her. Next, craft. I notice it is a simple question, and the refusal to answer it says more than a long speech. The strongest word is “digging”: it is the start of the new barn, the thing that will spark her revolt. Then, effect. Why does Sarah ask what the men are digging for? My answer: Sarah asks what the men are digging for because her husband makes major decisions without telling her; her question shows how little voice she has, which drives her to act.
